prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned Romanian prose, grounded in poetry, in which memory, the body and dream are built into a cosmological imaginative world that renews the inward and fantastic means of the novel.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: one prize part, one writer, Mircea Cărtărescu. The round-1 exchange did not weaken the grounds I gave, and the chair's questions let me state them more exactly. The case rests on a distinctive voice, a formal ambition that is carried at very large scale, and an imaginative project in which the intimate (body, memory, dream) is joined to the encyclopedic and extended across decades and across prose and poetry. On public knowledge, Blinding (the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid read as extensions of one imaginative scheme rather than repetitions of it, though I cannot confirm that from the texts. The case does not rest on nationality, political symbolism, or the fact that all six openings coincide. That coincidence is not literary evidence. In answer to the chair's question on citation scope, I have changed the wording only. It now names prose as the core and poetry as its ground, and it describes the renewal of the novel's inward and fantastic means. That is a literary description, and it avoids national symbolism. I would keep the language reference to Romanian because it describes the medium. Naming the language does not make a claim about the nation.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged and unresolved by the exchange. The claim of linguistic distinctiveness depends on Romanian sentence rhythm, long-sentence control and wordplay, which I cannot judge directly and which translation may flatten. No member has independent reading of the originals, so the whole-oeuvre judgment rests on reception and on the major novels. The later very long works may be uneven, and the committee has not produced specific evidence either way. Here is what would count against my position: credible assessments, such as translators' accounts or Romanian-reading readers' judgments, that the late volumes repeat the early architecture, or that sustained quality is concentrated in a few peaks. If that evidence appeared, I would look hardest at Wright, whose formal reinvention I find substantial, and at Carson, whose case depends on how the core oeuvre is defined.

responses.point: Olsson asks how the will's reference to an idealistic tendency applies to an inward, encyclopedic and often disturbing project, and says he does not treat the question as settled in either direction. He also keeps Carson second and ranks Wright last of his eight because the major novels are few.
responses.response: I agree the idealistic-tendency question is one of interpretation, and I would not treat it as an exclusion for Cărtărescu or for Carson without a shared reading first. My own tentative reading is that it concerns the orientation of the work toward human possibility and the dignity of the imagination, not a requirement of cheerfulness or consolation. On that reading, a project that treats the body and memory as the ground of a metaphysical inquiry is not disqualified by disturbing material. I offer this as a reading that colleagues can reject, not a finding. On Wright, I accept that corpus size bears on confidence about breadth over time. I would still not let it close the question, because scale, language and formal reinvention can carry achievement in a compact corpus. That is why she stays an alternative and not my choice.

responses.point: Mattson asks what Palm sees in Wright's whole body of work beyond Carpentaria and The Swan Book, and whether the later work and nonfiction deepen the achievement or only extend it. She also questions whether Carson's later work consolidates her breakthroughs.
responses.response: Her question is fair and I will answer it as far as public knowledge allows, without claiming to have verified it. As I recall, Wright's work includes an early novel, Plains of Promise, and nonfiction on Aboriginal politics. It also includes Tracker, a collective biography built from many voices and so an extension of the polyphonic method into non-novelistic form, and a recent large novel, Praiseworthy. If that is accurate, it suggests development of method rather than mere accumulation, but I cannot confirm that the later work equals the two central novels. So I would say only that the case is open and worth testing, not that it is established. On Carson, I would not call it a restatement merely because it returns to classical material. The returns appear to change the form each time, but that needs to be shown across volumes, and I accept that it has not been shown in this exchange.

responses.point: Carlberg ranked Wright sixth because a small number of major works makes sustained quality harder to establish. She asks to hear more about the later work, and she proposes that Carson could be defined as lyric and essay renewed through classical form, with translations as context.
responses.response: I share her view that corpus size is the difficulty and that the later work is the real test, and I have tried to say above what I understand of it. On Carson, I find her definition of the core useful. If the committee agreed that original verse, verse narrative and essay are the core and translations and scholarship are context, I think the case would be clearer and fairer to compare against Cărtărescu. I would still ask whether quality holds across many volumes and not only across Autobiography of Red and Nox and Nox. Until that is shown, I keep Carson as an alternative. I would not move her ahead of a project whose continuity across volumes I find easier to see, even if only through translation and reception.

responses.point: Swärd says the comparison between Wright and Cărtărescu turns on whether a compact corpus of two major novels can carry a whole-oeuvre citation as well as a longer, still-developing one. She adds that she is open to being persuaded by closer discussion of Wright's later work.
responses.response: I think that is the right way to frame it, and my answer is that for now a longer, more continuous body of work carries a whole-oeuvre citation more securely. That is why Cărtărescu is my choice, and why I do not move Wright above him on current evidence. I also note that she and I are using the same standard, form and language over symbolism, and arriving at different confidence levels because of corpus size. That seems a legitimate difference and I do not want to smooth it over. What I would add is that 'compact' should not be treated as 'thin', since the formal scale of Carpentaria is very large. The question is whether the evidence for development is enough, and I do not think it has been made yet.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg says that if the committee judged the later Cărtărescu work repetitive, Adonis or Carson would deserve a closer look. He also asks whether Arabic-language readers could settle what translation hides about Adonis.
responses.response: I agree that the late-work question is the one that could change the outcome, and I appreciate that he names what he would turn to. I do not think Adonis can be weighed fairly without Arabic-language assessment, as I said in round 1, and I ranked him lowest because of my limits and not because of a view on his achievement. I would add that the same logic applies to my own preference. If I accept that Arabic readers should be asked about Adonis, I should accept that Romanian readers should be asked about Cărtărescu, and I make the same request there. The asymmetry that Cărtărescu is more accessible to me in translation is a limit on my evidence and should not be mistaken for a literary advantage.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's effect depends on Romanian sentence rhythm and wordplay that translation may not carry. My judgment rests on public knowledge of the works and their reception, not on independent reading.
Whether the late, very long novels deepen the early project or repeat it. No member has produced specific evidence either way, and I cannot verify this.
Coverage of the poetry, early work and essays in translation is thinner than for the major novels, so the corpus is judged unevenly.
My recollection of Wright's later and nonfiction work is from public knowledge and is not verified, so the statement that it shows development is provisional.
How to read the will's reference to an idealistic tendency. My reading is tentative and is not a shared committee interpretation.
I cannot assess Adonis's Arabic prosody or Yan Lianke's Chinese prose, so any comparison involving them is asymmetrical.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The profile records institutional connections to the Academy and committee colleagues, but none to any shortlisted writer. My own practice with myth, fairy tale and ekphrasis, and my biography of Selma Lagerlöf, are context only and are not evidence of a preference for any candidate. Her status as a co-opted member in 2024 and a full member in 2025 is recorded in the profile, but the profile does not explain it. Nothing in this disclosure is adjudicated here.
